summary: Newark-built wooden Bearfort Mountain lookout, used 1916 to 1932 and destroyed by fire; a steel tower that replaced it still stands on the mountain.

facts.design: Totally enclosed wood lookout cab with inside stairway; height disputed (forty-foot frame per 1923 newspaper, 50-foot wooden per NHLR)
facts.status_note: Burned in 1932; a later 68-foot steel tower stands on the mountain (see us-nj-bearfort). No source describes remains of the 1916 wooden lookout.

events.note: Watcher on constant duty in a tower already standing on Bearfort Mountain under the Weeks Law agreement; predates the 1916 lookout
Wooden lookout built by the City of Newark for the Forest Fire Service; 1915-16 state report says the earlier tower was unfit; 1923 article gives 40-foot frame
Watchman continuously on duty in the city-provided tower from April to December
Destroyed by fire; believed to have started from stovepipe sparks; fire warden Charles Stalter on duty
68-foot steel tower built on the mountain after a tree platform interim (NHLR gives 1934; FFLOS gives 1937)
Registered on the Former Fire Lookout Sites register July 24, 2016, nominated by Robert Spear

resolved_conflicts.field: height and construction of the 1916 wooden lookout
resolved_conflicts.explanation: NHLR gives a 50-foot wooden tower; a 1923 newspaper item gives a forty-foot frame structure built in 1916 by the City of Newark. Both are reported; neither is chosen.

NHLR gives an iron-frame tower built in 1909 as the predecessor; the 1915-16 state report describes an earlier tower that had become unfit. The sources do not say whether these are the same structure, so it is left open.

resolved_conflicts.field: build year of the steel successor tower
resolved_conflicts.explanation: NHLR gives 1934; FFLOS gives 1937. Both dates are reported; neither is chosen.

notes_for_editor: Brief status 'gone' is right for the 1916 wooden lookout. The mountain still has the steel tower covered by us-nj-bearfort, so keep the two records apart. Height (40 vs 50 ft) and successor year (1934 vs 1937) conflict across sources; both are reported. The 1913 watcher entry refers to a tower already on the mountain; sources do not say whether it is the 1909 iron-frame tower. Access not classified because no source says whether the old site is open. Cached text has no image URLs, so no photos recorded; FFLOS and NHLR both caption a 1925 photo of the wooden tower.
